This is basically how I see it as a software developer. My industry has been completely upended by AI. I've not written an unassisted line of code in a year, and - with more than a little oversight - the code the models have written is as good as anything I could write manually. Certainly much faster. It's safe to say that if I could abstract my work into "units" of productivity, I've created far more units of useful code than I ever have. But a lot of that code is for things that I simply would never have even bothered writing in the past, either because the payoff (monetary and non-monetary) just wouldn't have made the effort worth it. Little utilities for my Mac, testing frameworks, simple games, automations of common tasks I used to do manually, etc. These are basically analogous to the pyramid example used in this video - useful stuff, but only really _viable_ as a thing to create once time/effort expended dropped below a certain threshold. There is a lot of stuff that has yet to be created because, in the age of artisanal fine-tuned code, it just didn't make sense to take the time to make it. This isn't new to software, really. Things like object oriented programming and automated testing also opened up doors to more complex and more niche software that would have been impossible or just plain uneconomical to make previously. I could wring my hands about being replaced - and if I didn't explore these tools and learn to become comfortable with them, I would be - but I'd much rather be building all of those new things that have been opened up.
